prompt: Under what conditions does an alkene react with N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) to give allylic bromination?

choices.text: In the presence of ultraviolet light
With a strong acid catalyst
choices.why: Allylic bromination with NBS is a radical chain reaction run in ultraviolet light, not an acid-catalyzed polar reaction.

choices.text: In the dark at low temperature
choices.why: The reaction is carried out in the presence of ultraviolet light, as in alkane chlorination.

choices.text: With added HBr, by a polar addition mechanism
choices.why: HBr adds across a double bond by a polar mechanism to give a Markovnikov product. NBS with light instead substitutes an allylic hydrogen.

explanation: Alkenes react with N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) in the presence of ultraviolet light to give products in which hydrogen is replaced by bromine at the allylic position. The reaction is analogous to alkane chlorination and occurs by a radical chain pathway.

prompt: Where is the allylic position of an alkene?

choices.text: At a carbon next to the double bond
At either carbon of the double bond
choices.why: Those are vinylic carbons. The allylic position is the carbon next to the double bond.

choices.text: At a carbon two carbons away from the double bond
choices.why: The allylic position is directly next to the double bond, not one carbon further.

choices.text: At the most highly substituted carbon in the molecule
choices.why: Allylic describes a position relative to the C=C bond, not the degree of substitution.

explanation: NBS substitutes hydrogen by bromine at the position next to the double bond, the allylic position. In cyclohexene, carbons 3 and 6 are allylic.

prompt: What is the main organic product when cyclohexene reacts with NBS in ultraviolet light?

choices.text: 3-bromocyclohexene
1-bromocyclohexene
choices.why: That would replace a vinylic hydrogen. Vinylic C–H bonds are the strongest (465 kJ/mol), so they aren't attacked.

choices.text: 4-bromocyclohexene
choices.why: Carbon 4 isn't next to the double bond. Bromination happens at an allylic carbon, carbon 3 or 6.

choices.text: trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane
choices.why: That is the anti addition product of Br2 across the double bond. NBS substitutes an allylic hydrogen and keeps the double bond.

explanation: NBS replaces an allylic hydrogen with bromine. Cyclohexene's allylic positions, carbons 3 and 6, are equivalent, so the product is 3-bromocyclohexene (85%), along with succinimide.

prompt: In the section's example, cyclohexene reacts with NBS in CCl4 under light. What percent yield of 3-bromocyclohexene is obtained?
explanation: Cyclohexene gives 3-bromocyclohexene in 85% yield, with succinimide as the other product. Bromine replaces a hydrogen at an allylic position (carbon 3 or 6).

prompt: How many allylic carbons does cyclohexene have?
explanation: The double bond joins carbons 1 and 2. The carbons next to it, 3 and 6, are allylic; carbons 4 and 5 are not next to the double bond.

prompt: What kind of mechanism does allylic bromination with NBS follow?

choices.text: A radical chain reaction, like alkane chlorination
A polar addition through a bromonium ion
choices.why: That is how Br2 adds across a double bond. NBS bromination substitutes an allylic hydrogen by a radical pathway.

choices.text: A polar reaction through a carbocation intermediate
choices.why: The intermediate is an allylic radical, not a carbocation.

choices.text: A single step with no intermediate at all
choices.why: It is a repeating chain of steps with an allylic radical intermediate (Figure 10.3.1).

explanation: Allylic bromination with NBS is analogous to the alkane chlorination reaction of Section 10.2 and occurs by a radical chain-reaction pathway (Figure 10.3.1), with an allylic radical as the intermediate.

prompt: In the first step of allylic bromination with NBS, what does the bromine radical, Br·, do?

choices.text: Abstracts an allylic hydrogen to give an allylic radical
Adds to the double bond, giving a bromonium ion
choices.why: Br· abstracts an allylic hydrogen. Bromonium ions form when Br2 adds to alkenes by a polar mechanism.

choices.text: Abstracts a vinylic hydrogen, giving a vinylic radical
choices.why: Vinylic C–H bonds are the strongest (465 kJ/mol) and vinylic radicals the least stable, so the allylic hydrogen is taken instead.

choices.text: Reacts with a molecule of NBS to form Br2
choices.why: It is HBr, formed in the first step, that reacts with NBS to form Br2.

explanation: Step 1: a Br· radical abstracts an allylic hydrogen atom of the alkene, giving an allylic radical plus HBr. Step 2: the HBr reacts with NBS to form Br2. Step 3: Br2 reacts with the allylic radical to give the bromoalkene and a new Br· (Figure 10.3.1).

prompt: What happens to the HBr formed during allylic bromination with NBS?

choices.text: It reacts with NBS to form Br2
It adds across the double bond to give a Markovnikov product
choices.why: In this mechanism the HBr reacts with NBS, making the Br2 that brominates the allylic radical.

choices.text: It reacts directly with the allylic radical to give the product
choices.why: The allylic radical reacts with Br2, not HBr.

choices.text: It is a by-product that takes no further part
choices.why: HBr is needed: it reacts with NBS to give the Br2 used in the next step.

explanation: The HBr made when Br· abstracts an allylic hydrogen reacts with NBS to form Br2. That Br2 then reacts with the allylic radical to give the brominated product and a Br· radical.

prompt: In the last step of allylic bromination with NBS, Br2 reacts with the allylic radical. What does this step produce?

choices.text: The bromoalkene and a Br· radical
A 1,2-dibromide and a Br· radical
choices.why: Br2 reacts with the allylic radical, not across the double bond, so the product is an allylic bromide that keeps its C=C bond.

choices.text: The bromoalkene and HBr
choices.why: Br2 gives one Br atom to the radical; the other leaves as Br·, not as HBr.

choices.text: The bromoalkene and a new molecule of NBS
choices.why: NBS isn't regenerated. The other bromine atom leaves as Br·, which cycles back into the first step.

explanation: Br2 reacts with the allylic radical to yield the brominated product and a Br· radical. The Br· cycles back into the first step and carries on the chain.

prompt: The section compares C–H bond strengths in cyclohexene. What is the approximate strength of an allylic C–H bond, in kJ/mol?
explanation: An allylic C–H bond has a strength of only about 370 kJ/mol (88 kcal/mol), compared with about 410 kJ/mol for a typical secondary alkyl C–H bond and 465 kJ/mol for a vinylic C–H bond.

prompt: A vinylic C–H bond has a strength of 465 kJ/mol and an allylic C–H bond about 370 kJ/mol. How much stronger is the vinylic bond, in kJ/mol?
explanation: 465 kJ/mol − 370 kJ/mol = 95 kJ/mol. Vinylic C–H bonds are the strongest of the three kinds and allylic C–H bonds the weakest, which is why NBS removes an allylic hydrogen.

prompt: A typical secondary alkyl C–H bond has a strength of about 410 kJ/mol, and an allylic C–H bond about 370 kJ/mol. By about how much is an allylic radical more stable than an alkyl radical with the same substitution, in kJ/mol?
explanation: 410 kJ/mol − 370 kJ/mol = 40 kJ/mol. Less energy is needed to form the allylic radical, so it is more stable than a typical alkyl radical with the same substitution by about 40 kJ/mol (9 kcal/mol).

prompt: Which of these kinds of radical is the most stable?

choices.text: Allylic
Tertiary
choices.why: Tertiary radicals are more stable than secondary, primary and methyl radicals, but allylic radicals are more stable still.

choices.text: Secondary
choices.why: Secondary radicals are less stable than both tertiary and allylic radicals.

choices.text: Vinylic
choices.why: Vinylic radicals are the least stable of all; vinylic C–H bonds are the strongest (465 kJ/mol).

explanation: Adding vinylic and allylic radicals to the ordering gives the stability order vinylic < methyl < primary < secondary < tertiary < allylic.

prompt: Which of these kinds of radical is the least stable?

choices.text: Vinylic
Methyl
choices.why: Methyl radicals are less stable than primary, secondary and tertiary ones, but still more stable than vinylic radicals.

choices.text: Primary
choices.why: Primary radicals are more stable than methyl and vinylic radicals.

choices.text: Allylic
choices.why: Allylic radicals are the most stable on the list.

explanation: The expanded stability order is vinylic < methyl < primary < secondary < tertiary < allylic. A vinylic C–H bond is the hardest to break (465 kJ/mol), so the vinylic radical is the least stable.

prompt: Why does bromination with NBS occur only at the allylic position and not elsewhere in the molecule?

choices.text: Allylic C–H bonds are weakest, so allylic radicals are most stable
The vinylic C–H bonds are the weakest, so they react first
choices.why: Vinylic C–H bonds are the strongest (465 kJ/mol); allylic ones are the weakest (about 370 kJ/mol).

choices.text: NBS first adds to the double bond, which directs Br to the next carbon
choices.why: NBS doesn't add to the double bond. A Br· radical abstracts an allylic hydrogen.

choices.text: Allylic hydrogens outnumber all the other hydrogens in the molecule
choices.why: Cyclohexene has as many hydrogens on carbons 4 and 5 as on its allylic carbons 3 and 6. The reason is bond strength.

explanation: Bond dissociation energies give the answer: a typical secondary alkyl C–H bond is about 410 kJ/mol and a vinylic C–H bond 465 kJ/mol, but an allylic C–H bond only about 370 kJ/mol. The allylic radical is therefore about 40 kJ/mol more stable than a typical alkyl radical with the same substitution.
